=== Canvas 8 (Prelim. 1v) ===
[Full Page]
When est[er] terme doth begyn .
Be yt knowen that est[er] terme doth begynne all ways the xviijth day aft[er] est[er]
[and] the same day for one and endyth the mo[n]day nexte aft[er] the ascen[ci]on daye .
Trinite terme doth begyn .
All way the fryday nexte aft[er] Corpus christi day: And endythe
the wensday fortnyght aft[er].
Michallmas terme doth begynne .
All way on the nynthe or tenthe day of October: And endyth
the eyght and thirty or nyne and twenty day of Nov[em]ber .
hillary terme doth begynne .
The three and twenty or foure and twenty of Januarye and endithe
the twelfte or thyrtyne day of the monyth of february .
Notte thys that in est[er] terme on the assencyon day: In trinyte terme
on the natyuyte of seynt Jho[n] baptiste: In mychallmas terme on
the feste of all seynte and on all soulles day: in hillary terme on candel
mas day: nor vppon any sonday: the kyng[es] Judge do not vse to sytt
in Judgment.
for the Carpe ether in pole or in the ryver.
Take a bayte that ys called a codde bayte & first put yo[ur] hocke thorow the mydle
of him: or any of the[m]: then put on, one on the poynte of yo[ur] hocke a longe wyse
and so angle w[i]t[h] thys & the carpe will byte at yt . . . . . . . . H .
To make a bait for to make a lake to fall [?]
Take the schewyngs of horne: and gud stronge worte / and boyle yo[ur] horne and yo[ur] worte to
geder tyll yt be as thyk as tylle: and then straine it on[e] lynnene clothe that shall be
new[e] wasche and then drye it well and then put yt into yo[ur] tube and so make it up.
for synewe ache ... dog[es] ... water
Stile. | Stile. | A trewe Est & weste erecte diall. | Another fassion Stile ...
Henry Dingley

Vere or springe time begynnthe whe[n] the sunne enterythe
into the signe of Aries: & it indures . 93 . dayes þ[a]t is fro þ[e]
xj day of marche vnto the . xij . of June . in this tyme the
day & nyght are evyned in his regione . þ[e] tyme waxithe
plesant & sweet, the ayre ys purified . the spryngys
boyle oute of the yerthe . the moystnes that in wynt[er] abode
in rotys astep up into the croppys of ev[er]y plante .
beste & fules renew hir kyndes . & fisshes go to hir spawn[n]g
& trees the[m]selfes: & bring furth their frutes in their
kyndes . the yerthe ys bewtified w[i]t[h] flours of freshe colors
& the tres w[i]t[h] flours & fruite . & all thing that berip lyfe is
refresshid . The worlde ys the[n] lykenyd onto a mayde
of . xvij . yeres of age that ys bewtifull bothe of face, body,
and all kynd of gorgi[us] apparrell . Veere is hoote and
moyste: & it is temp[er]at lyke onto the eaire . the blod
of man ys quykenyd and sterid a brode into all p[ar]tes
& me[m]bres of the body . & it sitop in that, that ys equale
in co[m]plexcon: that ys to sey te[m]perat . And in the time
of Veere thow sholdes eate henne: chekyns: capons:
& suche lyke: & new leide egge softe droste amonge that
ys to sey sildn: & eate wilde letuse . i . rasins: drinke
eate gott[es] mylke: for it resto[re]th natu[r]all breath . ther
ys no time of the yere more bett[er] or mo[re] p[ro]fytable
to blede in . & in that time labor & movynge of the
body ys good . to bathe, to provoke swete, to drinke
& eate sirupe made of spyce & of erbys that are semi
purat: and to take purgacyons ys god . H.

Estas or Som[er] begynn[eth] whe[n] the sunne enterith into
the firste degre of the Crabe: & it indurith . 92 . dayes þ[a]t
is to sey fro the . xij . of June vnto the . xiij . of septe[m]ber .
& in this time the days are lengthenyd . & the nyght[es]
shortenyth . and in all regions heet incressythe: the
windis are in flamyd by heet & drynesse: the se is pasa-
ble: stre[m]es are gederid: ven[n]m ys distroyed: the frutes
lyes welle in the strennyth & lepynge are flyes & venym
at their fode wher of they haue plenty . the eayre is
clere: corne waxithe rype: and the[n] the worlde is lyke
a spouse co[m]plett of body & of phy[si]c age in flamyd w[i]t[h] hoote .
The tyme of som[er] is hoote & drye in y[e] wiche reed coller
is raysid, exercisid & boudyn in boddies disposid . And it be
hovythe the to be ware of ev[er]y meate that is hote & drye of
co[m]plexion: for that excytythe reed coller . absteine that time
fro replecyon bothe of meate & drinke lest natu[r]all heete
be quenchid . But eate tho & such thinge that ys moyst &
colde of natu[r]: as vealle w[i]t[h] vineg[ar]: fatte chekyns: capons:
cucumbyrs: & suche other . yo[ur] pottage shulde be made w[i]t[h] the
brane of barley . in that tyme tho wiche are of soure taste
& sowaples dothe lesse hurte to the body . and in thys time
of som[er] for beare the lose of weens: lettinge of blode: &
baythes: and fro ovmiche movynge of the body . for all
thos thinge ar conselling to be ov[er]myche usid in this
tyme of som[er] . ideo ca[v]eas: et iter[um] dico tibi caue . H.

Hervfste begynneth whe[n] the sone enthorith into the first
degre of libra: & it indures . 89 . dayes þ[a]t ys fro the . 14 .
day of septe[m]ber: onto the . 13 . day of december in that time y[e] day
& the nyght are evenyd: & the nyght begin[n]eth to grow, & taketh p[ar]t
of the day . the eaire waxis colde: the wyndis blow: water wax:
the grene thinge of the yerthe wade: fruite & lewys falle: & the
bewty of y[e] yerthe, tres & erbis are gone . fowles fly into hote regions:
wildbeste seke hir denes: & spend hir dyches where they ged[er] fode
to susteine the[m] in wint[er] . the fyshes drawe towardes the depe place
of the ryv[er]s & wat[er]s . The[n] the worlde is lykenide onto a woman of
58 . yeres of age that hath nede of clothes, for youthe ys gone fro
hir . herufste is a time colde & drye: in the wiche blacke color &
slyp . Therfore it be hou[er]the the to eate: meate that are hoote & moyst
as chekins flessh: chekins: yonge donys: porke: w[i]t[h] powd[er] of ging[er]
& drinke olde wine of depe coullor: swete wine & eate swete grap[es]
pyes . and absteine fro all meate that inge[n]d[er] malencoly: as beffe:
gose: olde pygyons: porkes: soure grape: shepfyshe: ch[ese] & suche
other . Then put in exerc[ise] the movynge of the body mo[re] rather
the[n] in som[er] . vse bathes in this time yf nede be: & vse laxatiues: &
yf a man nede to have a veyn to let it be but a litel & that in the
hoottest howr of the day: for in suche howers of the day sup[er]fluitie
are gatherid in a ma[n] . allso the p[ur]gyn of the wome[n] ys to be vsyde
in that time . w[i]t[h] pill[es] callid dia[s]ene: & w[i]t[h] electuario rosat:
lapis lazuli: & ac[e]tum: & suche other as p[ur]gyn or dryvyn
owte blake color: and allso repress[e]th homor . H .
Septem[ber] hathe . xxx : dais .

Nox habet horas . xvj . dies vero . viij
hiems or Winter begynneth whe[n] the sone enterith into the
firste degre of the gote: & it indurith . 89 . dais that is to sey fro the . xiij . day
of dece[m]ber onto the . xj . of marche: in that time the dais ar shortenide
& the nyghte are lengthenyd: colde waxithe myghty: the windis wax
sharpe, the lewys of trees are felle: and all grene thinge for the
moste p[ar]te dieth . the moste p[ar]te of beste that are wilde do drawe into
cavys & depe place of the erthe: to kepe the[m] fro the bitternes of the
tyme, & eaire w[i]t[h] hoar darcke: beste bothe wilde & tame do knepe[n] in
den[n]s, & the strengthe of ther bodyes are wekenyd . the fyshes of fresshe
wat[er]s do draw into the dep[er]s and lurke in hallow banckes, & into great
scolles and all for fere of the wint[er]s colde . The[n] the worlde ys lykenyd
onto an olde woman nere naked goinge to deth . The time of wint[er]
is colde & moyste: in the wiche time yt behovyth to chaunge thy diet:
& to retorne to hoote meate & hoote substaunce . as chekins: henes: capons:
p[er]trige: fesant: bird[es] of the busshe & wilde & smalle: gote flesshe roste:
hogge flesshe: & lambis . all hote spices: & reed wine: figge & nutte: also
hote Electuaryes & syrupes: Absteine fro lossynge of the wombe
w[i]t[h] medissines: and fro lettinge of blode: excepte greatt nede require
yt . The[n] chaunge the eaire: that ys to sey drawe the into warme and
close place fro the colones of the eaire . a noynt yo[ur] body w[i]t[h] hoote & precius
oyngn[ent]es: & tepid bathys . Miche movynge of the body: nor the dedis of veny:
nor saden or miche eatinge hurt[e]th not . so that digestio[n] be not feblyd .
ffor in that tyme of g[re]at colde the natu[r]all heate is gatherid into the
in[n]er p[ar]te of the body: & therfore in wint[er] ys the digestio[n] beste . & in
Vere: & in som[er] the wether ys hote: & in thos times the powres are
openyd, & the natu[r]al heet dispeverid into all p[ar]tes of the body . and
for stantnes of heate the digestio[n] of the stomake ys feblyd and lettyd .
& homor are movyd to the extremyt[es] . gife god thank[es] of p[re]s[er]vatio[n] . H .

The weyghte the wyche ar moste in vsse at thys day Do ffollowe wrytte
The : 10 : day of Auguste ano xpo : 1564 : et ano vjto Elzabethe R[egi]n[a]e :
A pownd is wrytte thys . li : j . li : ij . etc . halfe a pownde is wrytten thys . li . s[emis] . or thys . li . d . or li . s .
An oince ys wrytte thys . ℥ . j . or ℥ . j . etc . halfe an oince ys wrytte thys . ℥ . s[emis] . or thys . ℥ . d . or thys . ℥ . s .
A . drame is wrette thys . ʒ . j . ʒ . ij . etc . halfe a drame ys write thys . ʒ . s[emis] . or thys . ʒ . d . or thys . ʒ . s .
A . drame & a halfe ys wrytte thys . ʒ . j . s[emis] . or thys . avreos or thys . aure .
A scrypul is wrytte thys . ℈ . j . ℈ . ij . etc . halfe a scrypul ys writte thys . ℈ . s[emis] . or thys . ℈ . d . or thys . ℈ . s .
A . handfull is writte thys . M . j . M . ij . etc . halfe a handfull is writte thys . M . s[emis] . or thys . M . d . or thys . M . s .
A lytell handful is writte thys : p . x . or pugillus . A greate handful is writte thys Manipulus .
A quarte of a pownd is writte thys . q[ua]rt[a] : or : q . halfe a quarte[n] ys writte thys . q[ua]rt[a] . s[emis] . or thys . q . d . or s .
A . Corne weyght or a grayne ys wrytten thys : grana : or thys gra : or thys : gr : or thys : g . or g .
And who ye moste take of eny one lyke myche or of eny one a lyke q[ua]ntite is writte thys : āā : or ana .
And thys fygure ffollowynge dothe sygnyfy gyng[er] . ℥ʒ : or thys ℥ʒ : or els thys . ℥ʒ . : j : gynger .
The leste of all weyghte com[m]enly vsid amonge physytyons ys a barly corne weyght : and : xx : good cor=
nes do make a : ℈ : and : iij . ℈ . do make a : ʒ . and . viij . ʒ . make an : ℥ . and . iij . ℥ . a q[ua]rt . and . xij . ℥ . make a : li .
Whore sew ye se this carecte . H . D . stand in the mrgent of this my boke agaynste any medyc[in]e / oyle /
oyntme[n]t / salue / playst[er] / water / powd[er] / sirrope / Electua[ry] / vngue[n]t / water / or any other thinge co[n]teynyd
w[i]t[h]in this boke that same I henry Dineley prouyde No other dowte & no other haue I my selfe p[ro]uyd . finis

Petra Philosophale . Phiorauant / agaynst all diseases
℞ Sill[er] miter, Rock allom, vitriall Romano ana
li j : first dry the vitriall in an erthen pan[n]e

wett closes upon ye head & receauer, bycause
the spirites shall nott flye awaye : the receauer
will wax red like bludd : and after turne whyte
and when ye geue it strong fier it will turne

and then it is ended kepe this close stopt in glas
to make ye petra philof[ophale]
℞ mercurie li j quick lyme ℥ vj comon

in thin plates ʒ j silver in thin plates ʒ ij gold leaues
ʒ j put them all to gether in the glas : and shake

=== Canvas 35 (Prelim. 15r) ===
[Left Column (Rod Bands & Soldering)]
I delighted in Angling & made my roddes my selfe
ffor white Tynne Bandes
Buy dubble plate and cutt it fitt for
yo[ur] cane and let it be a little to bigg
the[n] wrappe the sides ouer on an
other and make them rounde and
bind them a boute w[i]t[h] a wyer and
make them fitt and close to the cane
Then yo[u] must cut yo[ur] solder
in smalle thin peeces no bigg[er] than
little strawes — and laie it in the
inner side close upon the jointe
and putt a little fyne pulder of
Rasin upon the peeces of solder
Then holde the plate in the
flame of a candle and the taym
will melte and the solder run[n]
when it is run it is faste
Then washe the Smoke of the
candle off the out side and putt
it upon the cane: or scowre
it w[i]t[h] a cloute and sum Sande
y[e] yo[u] make boxes to put in hookes or other thinge
ffirste Solder the bande: then
cutt a square pece of plate a little
to bigge for the ende: and in the
iiij corners strike in holes: then
take iiij little peces of wyer and
make a hooke at on ende: put
that hooke upon the oute end of
the boxe and the other end through
the holes: and so thrust them all
abroade to holde the bottom faste
then laie on yo[r] peces of Solder
and Rasin then holde it ouer y[e]
candle & so make it runn in one
place first then in an other vntil
all be doone then w[i]t[h] a paire off
Sheares cutt of the plate rounde
and so yo[u] may mak the top[p]
ffor yallowe bandes
Buy dubble laten for poyntinge
cut them then binde the edges to
-gether w[i]t[h] wyer: then haue siluer
sowder cut so small as here — or elles
smaller and wet the brasse w[i]t[h] spettle
in the jointe then put on yo[r] sowder
in little peces: then put on Borax
in pulder a little all a longe: then
laie it in Burning cooles & blowe it
and yo[u] shall see it runn together
let it be oute of the fier and coole
the scowre it cleane: upon a lathe
is best w[i]t[h] a felt: yo[u] may do the like
w[i]t[h] lettes brasse: & it must be made
bright w[i]t[h] a file in a little lathe

[Right Column (Solder Recipes & Bait Paste)]
Ould pins of solid laten
very thin will solder well or yo[u]
may buy Siluer solder at the
gold smithes weight for weight
it is iij p[ar]tes siluer: one copper
white Solder is iij or vj
p[ar]tes leade and one or lesse off
Tynne: A pece of an old glasse
leade melted w[i]t[h] the pewter dish
is exelent good Solder
Good to other maide to do
white tynne bandes but heres
easie and finer enough
Both these sorte of bandes muste
be close in the joint as may bee
but the white may be the wider
of the leade
A paire of olde Tailors sheares
will cutt both
A Past to fyshe w[i]t[h]
℞ crumbs of white bred putt
them to water cullered yallowe
w[i]t[h] safron. put it in a dishe
pin it w[i]t[h] a pestle vntill it be
paste: putto a little Sugar in pulder
and pin it againe (it must be
very softe) then put it in a lead
boxe and hange it at yo[r] girdle
yf the water be cleare then
Strawe cullered past is beste
yf fowle water, then some
yallowe yo[u] paste
Note. yf yo[r] past bee to stiffe then
it is not good: for vnles the fyshe
when he pulles take some of the past
a waie he will not bite itt.
therefore make it so soft and
tender that yo[u] must take it out of
yo[r] boxe w[i]t[h] yo[r] finger and thumb
and put it betwixt yo[r] lippes &
so role it and then gentle put it
upon the poynt of the hooke: the
losse of the bayghte makes the fysshe
byte the better
Hauke crummes of white
bred and honye in a boxe in yo[r]
hande when yo[u] fysshe: yo[u]
must be liberall, and feed well:
and then they will byte & spring
past as a hen Egg is enough
at once yf yo[u] feede come to kede
A tynker tolde mee that sowder will runn and solder yallowe bands w[i]t[h] borax

[Left Column (Maturation Discourse & Poultices)]
When neyther Reprussion refrigeration
nor purginge will kepe the humor backe
but that hit must be ripened & broken
then doth hit turne an vlcer or foule
Soore . and being not well loked vnto doth
contynue longe before hit be heled And
many tymes turne into a fistola .
I haue herfore thought good for
to followe my intended course for the
maturation and Ripenynge of suche of
these humors as will not be Reprussed
And firste for the thinge whiche the
Cuntresse called cunnige women do
call takynge : whiche white, black or red
fauces : being in deed nothing but humor
settled in a place, & will not be striken
back, nor cooled, bycause ther came putti[ng]
therto scabbes or oyntments to them
and so suffred the humor to gett a head
and then must be ripened, and broken
& heled . w[hi]ch may bee doone twoe
wayes By pultesses off sundrie sorte
whiche must be applied hott & breake the
hede & abate paine or by oyntments
y[t] Maturatyues or ripenynge medecynes

I haue knowne sum lie xj or xiij
weekes w[i]t[h] a Bubo pentus and y[e]t
not breake itt .
Bubo is an ympostume in the
flanke so bigg as a Swannes Egg
and is gotten of corrupte women &
many tymes is of diu[er]s culors and
will stinke when it is opened
After a little tyme I found
it best to open them w[i]t[h] a knife &
tente them drawe them and hele
them as other sores w[i]t[h] maturatiues
mundificatiues and Sanatiues
it is more safe to open them w[i]t[h] caustick medecines
ffor where the skin is thick hit
is far better to open the Byle, bile,
Bubo, or ympostume then feare his
waight : for hereby the paine is much
abated and eased

Stupes the hed w[i]t[h] Sack: or co[n]fe[ct]
wyne or sharpe tiffle wett:
Then look for broken boones &
Spilles at the third or iiij dressing or
sooner yf neede bee
kepe the wounde close vnder the
Stupes from aire, and colde: and so
dresse him still without Salue
The harder the Stupes bee the
better the fleshe will gather
keepe the bare scull cleane from
filthe and suffer non of the ole[...]
to stick on the Scull
yf the fleshe growe proude
abate it w[i]t[h] the pulder of Sabyne &
nothing else
yf the newe fleshe seeme softe it
will harden well enoughe
yf the quarters knitte vpp at
the Bottom they will sinke lowe enoughe
in the ende therfore feare them nott.

Dry stitchinge of woundes.
When there doth happen greate cutts in
fleshe y[e]t is as in the calfe of the legge
or suche like the mouthes and egges of
the wound wilbe very wyde so that hit
wilbe very longe tyme to fill them w[i]t[h]
fleshe: then drye stitching is exceding
good and greate ease to the partie and
furthereth the healyng excedingly
ffor in stitchinge the fleshe in suche
a greate wounde the skin will not
holde to drawe the wound together
and if hit doo yet it will not holde
longe enoughe to the healynge.
In drie stitching I have often
observed hit that the cloute laide
on for plaster should be three square
and that s[h]ap[e] will hold the better.
To make the plaster ((
R[ecipe] towe peces of stronge lynen clothe
dubble them and cut the[m] after the
fashyon of three square, and let them
be longge and bigge enoughe for
the place then:
R[ecipe] good carpenters glue heat it so
good and stronge as yo[u] can gett it
and melt hit and put hitt apon
on side of y[e] plaster (but not neare
the dublyng) afterwardes all ouer,
then put the peces together and w[i]t[h]
a slik stone rubbe it gentle and
smothe itt. but put no glue apon
the one side: then put glue apon
the under most side [w]hich is plente
full and place the[m] on aboue and
the other under the cutt. then yo[u]
must bind them fast on w[i]t[h] a roler
and let them drie. then the next
morning stir the clothes w[i]t[h] a
dubble stronge thridd and drawe
it gently together and betwene
the thriddes dresse the wound w[i]t[h]
the twayt or turp[en]t[ine]: the verie
edges must have
no glue because
the nedle will
not bee thrus[t]
through it wil
bee so hardd ((

furnace of fyer: mary from the poynte
Susanna from the false cryme: Daniell
thou didest Deliuer out of the Lyons Den.
how didest Deliuer the Sunnes of abraham
how didest shew thi selfe in the hyenisse:
O Lorde Jesus Christ thou wast the first
man, that on leprens put apon:
Thi woundes did neither swell cankle,
aake, bleede, nor fester: So Lord Jesus
Christ, I beseche thee that theese sores
and woundes in this N. B. may neither
swell, kankle, aak, bleede, nor fester
but bee as whole, and as Sounde as
this woundes are. Lord for thi mercye
& for thi passions Saake Amen In
the name of the father &c &c &c.

86
Since I wrott the last medecine apon
the other side of the pin paper I haue tryd
vsinge the paper founde as followeth:
1° How the paper is painted
The painters haue a blew cullour w[hi]ch they
caule Litkmose and that ground in water
and temped with a weake sise is laid on the
paper and sheweth bluishe blew when
it is Drie: so they do itt and knowe the
cullor and haue so doone almost theese
threescore yeares: But what Litkmose
is made of I haue not yet learned:
CC. 2° The trew manner of Dressinge
y[e] broken shin w[i]t[h] it
Let the pacient wet the paper w[i]t[h] his
owne fastinge Spettle very wett. &
laie it on bigger than the Sore, and
be sure let it stick: (for it will not
lightly fall of) and take it not off
but as the Soore filleth w[i]t[h] matter and
a bunch ariseth vnder the paper, you
must thrust out the matter gentlie
with yo[u]r finger apon on side and let
the paper still stick. and abit healeth
the edges will rise where y[e] skin & fleshe
by the edges must be cut of: but yff
the paper break apon the Soore: then
put on a new pap[er] wet as at the first
w[i]t[h] fasting Spettle: So that comonlie
ij or iij papers heale the legge: And
when it is whole there is a little of
the pap[er] will stick on still: let it aloone
and this I neuer knew to prooue to
bee trewe: Deo gr[ati]as
And further yf there be an hole of a place
lower than the rest w[i]t[h] yo[u]r finger ye
must thrust downe the paper as it
doth stick on.

Broken Shines
I was much trobled w[i]t[h] Broken Shines &
it was that w[hi]ch my first made practyse
of cure thervnto the healinge wherof
caused many practises as appeareth in
theese Bookes and others.
1 ffirst I vsed Empl[astrum] Dingley
pa. 51 the Second Salue: which I did
applie vntill no speck of blud did cu[m]

and neuer tooke it of vntill it was all

Bubo in the Arsgutt
Bubo is an Impostume in the Arsgut or
Longanon, cu[m] greate hardnes & litle ache
at the firste, w[hi]ch is cu[m] oute pulsation
& in deed is a very canker: hit is nott to

How to know it
Lett the Chirurgion put his finger into the

stinking exceedingly

Soore Breste
℞ a Shepes head sett well on till Boile hit
in faire water a good quantitie thre or
fowre howres then lett the cleare water
run through a cleane clothe and into t[hat]
cleane water put in of cleane dight so
muche as will thicken it into the thicknes
of a thicke pultes and when it is thicke
Enoughe take it from the fire and stirr
in the yolkes of Egge[s] ij being first beten
well with a spoonefull of oyle of
Cammonill and mix them well all to
gether: Then aplie this pultes verye
warme but nott to hott all ouer the sore
being spreade on a thick clothe with a hole
cutt in the cloth for the nipple change
this plastor three tymes in # 24 h[ou]res
so that it may ru[n] of wett and moiste
nott drie in anye wyse. vide. 184.
And when the breste is broken then yo[u]
must haue Goates Dunge dried of
a gelded Goate, and made into fine pulder,
and Cersed, and mixe of that pulder
with pure huny but not made to thick
if the huny be harde then melt hitt
before yo[u] putte the pulder & that hit
may bee like a Syrop and beyond and
make a plaster of the huny and the
pulder (with a hole for the nipple)
and so dresse it morninge and Eueninge
that is twyse in 24 howres.
But you must nott tent the hooles in
any wyse: ~ vide 102 in fine.
Yf hit so happen that in healing of the
brest hit groweth harde or doth then
puffe or swell: then yo[u] must aplie
the pultes agayne: and when it is first
broken yo[u] must a plie the pultes two
or fowre dayes after before yo[u] lay
on your plaster of huny and goates
Dunge.
This did heale the ladie fitzgaroldes
brest when the Sargeant Surgion
failed of theire skill & the brest would
haue ben cutt of: and shee that did
heale itt had an hundred poundes
for her cures / vide. 184.

warme: this seemes as good as w[i]t[h] pulder
After xxx or xl yeares practis, I found
¶ that the often changing the plaster did
hinder the cure, & then I changed itt
on[e]s in euery fourte dayes: And when it
did it greater cure did ij or iij s[u]ch dayes
and hit cured it better in my mynde &
w[i]t[h] iij or iv plasters finished the cure.

[Upper Full-Width Section (De Panaritio)]
159
De Panaritio
Panaritio est Apostema callida accidens in latere vnguis vehementis
doloris & quandoq[ue] vlceratur & perducit ad corrosionem: & quandoq[ue] currit
Sanies ex vlceratione subtili & fetida & tunc est timor digiti
Cura
In principio emorgetur in aceto callido, mixto cum farina hordei: postea pone
hoc Empl[astru]m ℞ Draganthei vsti, thuris ana ʒj flori[s] aeris ʒfs agregantur
cu[m] melle et sup[er] pone: Si fuit corrosium humor tunc administra Calcadion
pa 42: Quando vlceratur impone aloes cu[m] Arsenico in modu[m] emplastri siue in
pulvere: et cooperiatur cu[m] panno imbuto in vino. Et quando incipit currere
Sanies ex panaritio vlcerato, tunc cauleria et munda vt non perambulet [et]
malitia in toto digito. deinde cura donec sanetur. hedes [?] no[n] aplicetur oleo [etc.]
Si vnguis corodat vt ius cu[m] cepacare [?] ℞ Cerusum et emisc[e] cu[m] pulu[ere]
auripigmenti et Emplastru[m] m[o]do facto sup[er] pone vnguij. M[agiste]r Joh[ann]es Arderon ad idem.
He writeth that a woma[n] hauinge a stroke apon the thumbe w[i]t[h] a mallet & [it] did
roote not heale it w[i]t[h] Sanguobolus pa 78 neyther w[i]t[h] vnguentu[m] viride, nor w[i]t[h] puluis
rubeus: But was enformed w[i]t[h] a hott yorne so fare itt y[e] & then heled itt.
This disease Panaritio is called a wyteflawe & it is a daungerouse e[vil]
and hott ympostume: and will eate the boone in the fingers end quite away in
a shorte tyme as I haue often seen and out of the one Jointe to hand the rest of
the hand when others haue bin longe about itt & could not do it:
I healed them as follows and failed not if they came in tyme Deo gr[ati]as

Synues pricke or hurte
I haue many that tooke on them greate
skill when a Synue hath bin prickt or els
parterwese [?] sume synue: that after xij days
or more with dressinges haue not bin heled
and the reason as I conceiued was ffor
that they could not stoppe a certen kind
of watrie Bludd that yssued furth from
the Synue hurte or cutt: which maye
be doon by digestiues to turne the blood
into quitture .i. thick white yelowe
matter. and so heale ytt vppe vide 139.
¶ If the syne putr[ify] or of white
Sugar be putte the Synue pricke to ytt
will make the humor issue & cause y[e]
wetinge of the Synue t[o] cease & it will
heale well after by digestion vid[e] 349
¶¶ But in a desperate cause you
may do thus

dissolue them put in this water

Cutting Ruptures
Take fyne hargold flax & make
therof a broad playet t[he]n spread
theron the whyte of an egge well
beaten: theron strewe y[e] fine
pulder of Bole vntill it bee
thoroughly wett & redd. then in y[e]
middest of the playet cutt a hole
to thrust the yearde throughe
make also a tente of the
almost as bigge as a mans little
finger, w[i]t[h] a longe threede att
the ende and dresse it like to
the plagett w[i]t[h] Bole &c the long
threede doth serue to pluck out the
tente furth of the codd.
Then take vpp the codd betwixt
the fynger and the thombe &
holde it fast w[i]t[h] the lefte hand
and lett an other hold the other
side fast and straine y[e]t hard
abrodt: then w[i]t[h] the knife cutt
a good round slitt in the skin off
the codde. then let the codd
be laied abroad fflatte.
Then open y[e] hole and gather vpp
the ryphacke w[i]t[h] y[e]r fingers and
holde it faste in y[e]r hande
To holde wher y[e] gutte came out
beinge taken vpp gather it all
towards the necke of the yearde
wher it is fastened and where
w[i]t[h] y[e]r thombe naile break ytt
off w[i]t[h] the veine of the garter y[a]t
groweth ther: take the greateste
paine to endure.
Then be sure y[e] hole faste the
ryphacke
Then haue y[e]r ligature reddy y[a]t
is fastened take ij pines & for a
double thread of good lynnen (well
waxte w[i]t[h] yelow wax) and
holde it fast at one end w[i]t[h] youre
righte hand: and let an other pat[ient]
holde the other ende and cast ytt
aboute the ryphack w[i]t[h] y[e]r holde
in y[e] lefte hande as neare the
botom as y[e] can & pluck ytt as
hard as may bee. and cast ytt a
boute twise or thryse & knit it fast
then cutt the threeds longe off and
let it lie in the cod or purse.

Hernia
Then put in y[e]r tente into the codd and
lett the little threede hange oute: and
put on the plaget to stope the bludde
and put ouer ij or iij lynen clothes
apon the plagett cutt as yt is.
But firste cutt of the ryphak
wher y[e] did hold in y[e] lefte hande
close by the bounde of the ligature
as y[e] can possible even hard to the
knott of the ligature
Note well whether the stone
cume w[i]t[h] the ryphacke or nott y[e]f it
do kepe him close for beinge seene
And thus lett him pair lie all
that daye and nyghte
Apon the morowe bath him w[i]t[h] sod[den]
mallowes in water kep[e] y[e] synues
warme and somewhat hott to kepe
yt from swellinge and so you
must doo other dayes.

w[i]t[h] the yolke of an egge and turp[en]tine

apon w[i]t[h] a tente

after assaye the ligature whether it

yt cu[m] of w[i]t[h] drawinge get him to

for sumtyme the ligat[ure] ca[n] not
as sone that sun[der] other
The ligat[ure] and the dead cure is doone
t[he]n heale the cutt in the purse

Duringe w[i]t[h] him let him kepe goodd

and get it good to purge & emptie

Beware of colde drinke and taking
cold in any wise:.
This was taught to mee by one
that was very skil[lful] man and
I see him dooe ytt to three
others: but bycause I was
knowne her[e] I wold not do itt

[Right Column]
☾ ☾ How I gott in the Bowels when they were harde & very paynefull ☾ ☾
Spreade sum of this forerem[em]b[ered] plaster apon a table napkin of linnen like linnen: and then warme git a little & wrappe the codd therin. Then let one w[i]t[h] a softe hande take the codd and let gutte wall gently into y[e] body in a very gentle kynd ☾ ☾
But if the pacient be fatt and the gutte be oute that ther is no roome for him: or yffe by straine hanging in the codde be hott & swellinge y[e] gutte so y[at] they will endure in or nott tary in by any meanes ☾ ☾
But if the gutte bee out mi[s]used & be come of wind or cold air to run hard and full of paine or hett or Burunge this plaster will take the paine away ☾ ☾
Or yf y[ou] haue nott the plast[er] redy then bray Rosemary & Smallage berry first coped small w[i]t[h] the grease aforesayd and applie git as aforesayde & git will do git as I haue often prouide ☾ ☾
And sumtymes by reason of the costiuenes of the p[atient] the gutte wilbe hard and paynefull. then the must be mad soluble as in page .5. 22. quicke salu[e] &c. ☾ ☾ ffor this purgeth him when an howre and a my[nute] and afterwarde medecyns maye downe at any tyme w[i]t[h]out drede.
An other waye to get vpp the gutte
℞ A lyve hen, a lyve catt, or a lyve whelpe; slitt him throughe the midle and applie gitt all hott and when it is cold put git into hott water and applie git againe and this do vntill it goe vppe. I alwaies used that before.

Discenteria
There bee iiij maners of fluxes
1 Dissenteria is when on[e]
doth bludd mingled w[i]t[h] ot[her] it were
the scrapinges of Gutte
2 Diarhoia the Bluddie
fluxe is when bludd passeth from
a man w[i]t[h] out mingling w[i]t[h] any
thinge like scraping
3 Lyenteria is when the
meate run[n]eth from a man all
whole and vndigested
4 Symple fluxe is when
one is solubel of that whiche
ytt hath eaten &c. and as it is
digested and thinne
There bee three maner
of Dissenteries
1 In the over gutte
2 In the midlemost Gutte
3 In the nethermost gutte
In on[e] it is like the washinge off
flesshe & is sone heled
In one other like scrapinge of gutte
or pergement
In the third it run[n]eth like to
whole gobbetts & is often tymes
incurable.

[Left Column (The Virtues of Oil of Vitriol — Wodgate)]
The vertues of Oile of vitrioll
♁ wodgate
It helpeth the Infirmyties of the Lyghtes,
w[i]t[h] ffenell or fumatory water. yt doth
putt away the melancolie humors from
the Stomake, w[i]t[h] Balme water. And doth
comforte the Stomake after a wonderful
manner, and doth defende the whole
body from Inwarde Apostumes & Infla
=mations. And therefore is vsed in y[e] plurisie
and in wound Drinkes & proued good
for it attenuateth the blud wonderfully,
and defendeth the ylls from corruption
and putrefaction
It conglutinateth Ruptures of boones and
veynes: and comforteth & strengtheneth
all p[ar]tes of the body exceedinglie & is a
principall cordyall
It preuenteth the Scorbutum taken inwarde
w[i]t[h] wyne or beare & is good in the spalme &
if it must be daylie vsed ij or iij droppes
In y[e]t callenture it appeaseth all other
medicynes taken in planten Surrell or
any other Colinge water or in the mydway
y[e]t they beinge lose bodyed phlebotomy vsed
In rotten and putrefyed Gumes totuge
the gumes gentlye onto w[i]t[h] the Oile: But
touche not the whole fleshe
In Angina and vlcerations in the throate
and mouth, that will not obey other med[i]c[ines]
touche it once w[i]t[h] this oyle warely & then
it will heale w[i]t[h] any med[i]c[ine] y[e]t
It is good for Inflamations in the throate
as Squinantia or Angina A fewe droppes
in a litt[le] Gargarismus or lotion. to make
sunne[s] hony sauor: put a fewe droppes. And
the body to ye Saluate
In vlceres and fistules to enlarg an orifice,
remoue a callous, to prepare it vnto
healinge: Dude touche it w[i]t[h] linte wett
in the oile apon a probe End
yt is good in al purgatiue medecynes
and diuretik workinges
It is good for a weak stomak opressed w[i]t[h]
flegme or slyme and in ex[cessive] conserue of
Roses a fewe droppes to turne the colour
it is Exelent in that case
In pestilentiall feuers it is exelent as m[r]
callend[er] a loud seide appeareth & on
the other side
The litle doz is so much as will make it
tast sumwhat sowre. In pestilentiall
feuers and callentures yo[u] may giue more
but Remember to shake it well before
yo[u] giue it for it will sinke to the bottom
Ant hath other vertues
the ♁ mark for oyle of vitrioll.

=== Canvas 287 (249) ===
[Left Column (Epileptia: Causes, Types & Signs)]
Epileptia
The Epilepcy or fallyng sicnes
cu[m]eth of a moyste humor thatt
filleth those places of the heade y[t]
shoulde be voyde, & stoppeth the
hynder parte of the heade, wyche
as is the begynnynge of the syknes
and filleth the Synues: And therfore
when this accide[n]t of the Sicknes
doth cume to a man it maketh him
for a tyme to loose his feelinge,
and his mouinge
Otherwise this sicknes
cu[m]eth of an humor in the heade
and then it is cauled Epilentia
Sumtyme yt cumeth of
fumes that flie into the heade
out of a feble and sick stomacke
and then it is cauled analeptia
Yf hit cu[m] of infirmytie of
other membres then it is cauled
cataleptia
There are ij Sortes of Epileptia
the greater &
the lesser
In the greater the principall
places of the Brayne are stopte
wherfore in theire acces they
feele nothinge and foome at the
mouth, and all the body quaketh
& they are hard to helpe
In the lesser the principall places
are not altogether stopped, & ther
fore in theire acces they feele sum
thynge and all the body quaketh not
but the hynder part of the hed
The tremblinge of the body is an euell
Sygne in the Epileptie And yf they do
fall often and aryse quyckly the sygne
is the better for their helpe
Yf a woman have this Sicknes and
was not healed before she have her
sicknes and naturall courses she
will never be heled this is yf hit
cu[m] to her in her childehoode
Yf the Sicknes cu[m] of humors
in the hedde these are the tokens
Heauynes of the head, the
confusion of his wytt, Slouthfulnes
Dymnes of his Eyes, Byting of the
tonge: theire water, nature, & siege
passe inuoluntarye, and in the greate
Epilepsie they ffall and feele nothing

[Right Column (Falling Sickness: Analeptia & Cataleptia)]
ffallyng Sicknes   249
Yf this sicknes cu[m] of flegme hit is knowen
hit is knowen by the Softenes, whitnes
sloute and muche sleepe
Yf of malencholie by blacknes
leannes, & such like
Yf it cu[m] of Both then the Signes are
mixed of bothe
§ Analeptia cu[m]eth of fume or
Smoake in y[e] Stomake: or els off
malencholie: the tokens are
Abhominat[i]ons to meate and drink
the trembleinge of the harte: p[ri]cking
of the Stomake.
fflegmatique meates and meate
that bre[d] malencholie do them muche
hurte.
Sumtymes they fall nott but are
feeble and weake aboute the tyme of their
acces
This sicknes may be of flegme
choller and mallenchollye And yow
may knowe of w[hi]ch by their signes
Cataleptia cu[m] of Smoak that
flieth faste of into the heade and there
ytt is colde: and this Smoake cu[m]eth of
a Bludde w[hi]ch maketh a man hott and
burninge w[i]t[h]out furie: and to have
a Swifte pulse: and often tymes hit
maketh him Sounde: and sumtymes
they have a feuer w[i]t[h] itt: and aunsiver
nott, when they are spoken vnto, and
yt is yuel to them to speake: their
Eies water, they Sighe muche: And
sumtymes their breth Stinketh:
In any of these three Sicknesses if the
pat[ient] foome much and white, and straine
their teeth hard when they are fallen
then the disease is of flegme
Yf he close his Eies as though he did slepe
and fome nott, and aryse quicklie it is off
choller.
Yf he wax blacke & turne his mouth a side
and straine his hands to gether: and lie
still as though he were deadd and
foome a little then it is of malencholly
They w[hi]ch have the Epi[lepsia] or Ana

Sup[er]fluitas carnis in naso co[n]surgens est
aliquando polippus, et aliquando non est
polippus, sed videtur esse; nam in ampliori
p[ar]te nasi fit, et exit aliquando nasum, et
sup[er] nos[trum] Labium moratur: cui[us] rei cura est
talis [pilcrow] Cum Spatumino p[er] q[u]a[n]da[m] pro=
funditatem eleuatur; et cum Sagittella
incidatur, & opertet inter palla fiat. et si
infra nares aliquid remanserit: tenta de
vnguento Ruptorio quod fit de
calce viua et Sapone Spataconitid et
fuligine, intromittatur. Deinde vitello ou[i]
cu[m] oleo co[m]munj mixto intingatur tenta,
et immittatur Postea vero ignis ces=
=sauerit, curetur ut vlcera puluera cu[m]
vnguento viride &c
Si vero fuerit inter nares tota caro, et
fit magna opilacione: Secundum modum
foraminis primo intromittatur tenta
mali terre succo, semel, bis, vel ter si fue=
=rit necesse: postea curetur ferro callido
vell Vnguento Ruptorio vt supradictu[m] e[st]
Polippus est quedam mala caro
intra nares crescens, cuius plures sunt
species Est quedam p[olippus] qua[si] inf=
=rub[ra] in corpore et sic dicit[ur] a Differtensione
for: quod est pluri[m]u[m] tenax quamuis est
molis substantie: talis mucus mouet nare[s]
concauitate naris, sensim separatur
vndiqu[e] a narib[us], non adheret, sed cum
p[er] minima quantitate, non possit exire
ibi existens opilat nares et foramen
precedens paulatim: et ita est incurabilis
Est alia species polippi omnino
adheret calorem, et est mollis: et illa
sedet in concauitate naris, que i[m]missis
vesitellu[m] potest rapi:
Polippus incurabilis h[e]c sunt
Signa: Locus niger, totus nasus dur[us]

=nis non descendit in for[a]me[n] n[e]c mouet[ur]
sed plurimu[m] crescit ibi in ess[e] sursum
Polippus q[u]i musc[us] no[n] assimilatur
Sic curatur
Nasus sursum frontem versus compri=

[Left Column]
In pa: 337 I wrote of ffractures but
since I see other practises and bicause
I haue written them vnseasonablie I
thought fitt to wryte them to gether
ffirste take measure of the biggnes of the
Legge: then prouide Splints cut them
and of conuenient length to the place
then Arme the splints w[i]t[h] flax w[i]t[h]out
sheles for pricking the fleshe: And
make thinge[s] to cumpas the legge
rounde aboute: but on[e] splint muste
not touche an other but there must
bee a little space betweene:
Then you must haue sum
holsters as in pa 337 :
you must also haue a strong lie made
reddye of faire water, w[hi]ch water ye
must make seethinge hott before ye put
in your Ashes, with sum of these herbes
followinge vizt: ffenell roote, iuniterum,
worme wod, Rose mary, Sage, camomil
flowers, or mellilote flowers: or sum
of theese: then put in y[ou]r Ashes and so
make y[e] lie slippie: then dreane y[e]
herbes and ashes from the lie And put
in good store off Salte when the lie
is cleane, and not before
Then take a good clothe, iij or
4 foldes, and wett in the lie hott and
and wring the clote harde: th[e]n lett
the clote be smothe, wrapped aboute
the broken legge very smothe w[i]t[h]out sea=
=ame or wrinkelles and hott:
Before the clote be put on le[t]
sure the bone be placed right
where it shold bee: And that yo[ur]
holsters fitt it nott:
This fowre folded clothe must
bee so long that the Endes of the

nott apon the bare fleshe.
The Edges of y[e] clothe muste
meete to gether and wrapp ouer
apon the topp of the shin boone w[i]t[h]
out seam[e]s knotte or bunches .
Then take an other duble clothe
wett in water and vinegar (if ther
bee cause:) wring hitt hard and laye

Now all theese thing[e]s being made

vnder the legg: and bind it att the
ouer Ende slacke: then laie downe the

ffirst put the End of on[e] splint
vnder the band alredi slacklie

at either End ij and ij in the middle
Remember the[y] touche nott on[e] the

Salve sanz Pere
319
quare non potest fieri Saniei generatio, et p[er]
quem non plagar[um] purgatio sed humores su[per]=
=flui ad plagas currentes retinentur & agra=
=vantur magis: hat magis p[er]inde tumor in plaga
augmentatur et somnus dolor. Quia alter
alterius est occasio quare plaga vel ulcus
indurescit, et tabescit et tabescit. Et pro
Sanie que in imo natura debebat effundere
quasi aquosum et virulentu[m] humorem emittit
Et sic multoties ex levi lesione,
incurabilia mala perpetrantur.
Unde Gallenus non revalescit plaga que sepe
transfertur. Et Hippocrates dicit raro sunt
removenda et rarius lavanda in quo medicamina
frequenter removentur.
Vulqus tamen alegant causam id=
=putant tales sedulos esse diligentes & sedulos
cu[m] potius sint magis p[er]niciosi ut in parum
laborant cognoscerent.
Dicunt em[im] tempus calida et plaga fortiter
currit, quod sepius removeri debet et host bis
vel ter in die, quia talis opinio partam sanie[m]
impidit, includit, quare sanies vel sanies
non tantum fetid[a] reddit[ur] vel fetorem facit
et tanto peius: mala sunt salutaria ad que
purgant humores aucti, calor em[im] accident[alis]
ad conversionem in Saniem. Sanies enim est
maxima presumptio Sanitatis.
Sanies enim cu[m] rel[iquis] Sanguis cu[m] humoribus
corruptis et calor naturalis diuista est, ergo
qu[ando] pulchra bona
Cruda vero et indigesta mala.
Et etiam aliter error in crebra remotione
plage vel ulceris: quia aerem nolunt ipsis
su[per]poni mutati p[re]cipue et p[er] consequens plagas
v[e]l desolitu[m] mulier[es] menstruosis.
alia, copa, remissa.
Quando plaga bene coler[et] & bone saniem emittere
videtur: & tumorem in o[mn]i p[ar]te existente
evanescere, et dolorem mitigari, et ad sibi
pristinu[m] et calorem remanere: non debet
dubiu[m] quin si par bene regatur (ut decet)
salus est expectanda. Hoc et pus in noctibus
bene decernit. In Somnis enim operatur
natura melius circa digestionem causs libet
materiem corpore aut in membra existentem.
Assidue inter impedit ut somnus do=
=res dolores, et ideo laboratur pro omnibus
ut dolor mitigatur.
Et scias quidem omnis natura est
operatrix, medicus vero minister.
Comendet ut anima bene memorie
qui et duca sunt de remotione plagar[um]
in pluris casibus non solitum removeri
nisi de tertio in tertiu[m] p[er]t[er] p[ri]ncipiu[m] in
lesionibus tibiar[um] q[uo]d ne sepe accedit in capite
sine peri.

Scorbutu[m]
The Scorby ys a Cronical dysase, not
Simple but compounded of many other
Infirmyties and therfore begyn the cure
by openny[n]g obstructions: therfore geve
him a lenetyve Clister [...]
Then let him blood a little, the next day
yf hee be stronge geve pille Rufi and
feede him good spoone meate: and in his
drinke infuse dryed wormewoodde
And geve him diatrion piperon
first and laste
mithridate, London [treacle] & pomis are good to
yeten fastinge. Aqua vite rosm[ar]i[ni] & the
Sun and currants are good & y[e] wone
Ginger &
And purge him with pills of
Euforbiu[m] ℈ iij or . ʒ . ss . theese purge cold
watery humors both by siege and vryne
and by heate geve[n] warmthe to the stom=
make and intralls: yf the stomak only
be opressed geve him pille Rufi . ʒ . j
Swetinge is good, therfor yo[u]
may geve him mithridate, or sum good
Treakle ʒ j and sweate him not w[i]t[h]
to many clothes
but to keepe him soluble

fenygreek brused ana ℥ ss boileth ana

picra . ʒ . ij Salt a little spoonfull: but yf

Another clister
of Beefe broth lb ij lyne seedes . ʒ ij the

ana ʒ ij boile them well then ad oile &
honye ana unc[ia] . j . And geve a pinte
Y nowe milke the yolke off
one egge and course suger is a good
gentle clister:
Suppositors may be used
℞ a long peece of Allom & pare it smoth
or the end of a candell, or a pece of
harde sope, so big and long as a
finger: and thrust itt upp . anoynted
w[i]t[h] oile or butter: or hony and salte

Note: yf y[e] p[ar]tie have the gutt
to bee clung, and harde: put a

yox  Singultus
Singultus yoxinge cometh dyverse
wayes: as of to muche Eating and drinking
and this yoxinge cometh comonly after
the Eating and drinkinge: this may
holpe by making the ptie agast, affrayed
or ashamed, disdayned, or right gladd or
by thrusting his fingar into his throate
holding him toward a thing uneles
And yoxing may cu[m] of corupt humors
in the stomake, that maketh the stomak
weake & feble and this yox cometh rather
before meate then after And this may
bee holpen by vomityng or purging
the offending humor. And then after
geve him good meates and drinkes
Lett him beward of surfetinge.:
Sumtymes it cometh of colde
in the ouer p[ar]te of the Stomake
and maketh that parte not hable to
delyuer the corupte humors that
are in the Stomake
Sumtymes of wynd and feeblenes
in the stomake and that may bee in twoo
manners. eyther of cold wycked hum[o]r
or of sum sikenes, as a flux or a fever
and when it is of a fev[er] it is daungerus
